meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The way to do is to be'?
meta.ogDescription: The exact wording is the last line of Witter Bynner’s 1944 Tao Te Ching (ch. 47) — popularized by a 1968 warehouse-wall graffiti chain.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: fl. 6th century BC (traditional) · semi-legendary Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
answer.sourceLine: These exact eight words are the closing line of chapter 47 in Witter Bynner’s 1944 “American version” of the Tao Te Ching — a free, poetic rendering, not a literal translation. The thought traces to Lao Tzu’s chapter 47, but the memorable phrasing is Bynner’s, and the line only became a stand-alone “quote” through 1968 Texas graffiti.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Witter Bynner, The Way of Life According to Laotzu: An American Version (John Day Company, 1944)
Texas warehouse graffiti, reported in the Dallas Morning News, 29 Jan 1968
Genuine translation line — but Bynner’s phrasing, not Lao Tzu’s literal words

source.excerpt:
There is no need to run outside
For better seeing,
Nor to peer from a window. Rather abide
At the center of your being;
For the more you leave it, the less you learn.
Search your heart and see
If he is wise who takes each turn:
The way to do is to be.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the stand-alone quote to a 1968 graffito: businessman Bud Crew wrote “The way to do is to be.—Leo-tzu” on a warehouse wall, per columnist Paul Crume in the Dallas Morning News, 29 Jan 1968.
A salesman answered underneath — “The way to be is to do.—Dale Carnegie” — and an anonymous wit capped it with “Do be, do be, do.—Frank Sinatra,” per Quote Investigator.
The eight words are real, though: they close chapter 47 of Witter Bynner’s 1944 translation — a rendering scholars treat as creative interpretation rather than literal Lao Tzu.
Tao specialist Stefan Stenudd files it among questionable Laozi quotes, noting it is Bynner’s wording and reads more like wordplay than wu wei.
source.excerptNote: Chapter 47 in Witter Bynner’s 1944 rendering. The famous line is the stanza’s final clause; lifted out alone, it reads as an epigram Bynner never intended it to be.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is a 1944 translation line by Witter Bynner (1881–1968), first published by the John Day Company — well after 1931, so it is in copyright in the United States, held by Bynner’s estate/foundation and publisher. Lao Tzu’s ancient Chinese original is long in the public domain, but this particular English phrasing is not.

author.name: Lao Tzu
author.heading: About Lao Tzu
author.metaLine: fl. 6th century BC (traditional) · semi-legendary Chinese sage · reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (Laozi, “Old Master”) is the semi-legendary Chinese figure traditionally credited with the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism. His actual existence and authorship are debated by scholars, and the surviving text is a compilation whose exact wording depends entirely on its translator. Chapter 47 — the source of this line — counsels inner cultivation over outward striving, but says nothing so epigrammatic as “the way to do is to be” until Witter Bynner phrased it that way in 1944.

misattribution.heading: How a 1944 poet’s line became “ancient wisdom”
misattribution.intro: The line is posted everywhere as timeless Lao Tzu, but its real path runs through a modern American poet and a Texas warehouse wall.

items.who: Witter Bynner (1944), not Lao Tzu himself
items.why: These eight words are Bynner’s closing clause for chapter 47 in his self-described “American version.” Literal translations of the same chapter render nothing like this pithy epigram, per the side-by-side comparison.
Quote Investigator finds its fame began when businessman Bud Crew chalked it on a warehouse wall crediting “Leo-tzu” — reported in the Dallas Morning News on 29 Jan 1968.
The wall grew a wordplay chain — “The way to be is to do” (pinned on Carnegie) and “Do be, do be, do” (on Sinatra) — none of which those men actually said, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Lao Tzu’s chapter 47; the memorable eight words are Witter Bynner’s 1944 phrasing, launched into pop culture by graffiti — not a literal saying of the ancient sage.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Bynner didn’t read classical Chinese; he built his 1944 “American version” from an earlier scholar’s guidance and his own poet’s ear. The result is beloved for its grace but is treated by scholars as creative interpretation rather than a faithful translation — which is exactly why a memorable line like this one has no counterpart in more literal renderings.

Lifted out of its stanza and stripped of Bynner’s name, the clause reads like an ancient one-liner. The 1968 graffiti chain did the rest, welding it to “Lao Tzu” in the popular mind decades before it reached today’s quote sites.
context.pull: The idea is Lao Tzu’s; the eight words are Bynner’s.
